items.prose:
A loader checks the vendor's file before computing returns.

```python
prices = [100.00, 0.00, 105.00]
assert all(p > 0 for p in prices), "zero price in file"
print("loaded")
```
items.question: What happens?

options.text: It stops with `AssertionError: zero price in file`

options.why: You missed the £0.00. One price fails `p > 0`, so `all` is False and the assert stops the script.
A false assert raises an error. It never prints the condition.
Nothing is divided here. The assert stops the script before any return is computed.

feedback.correct: The £0.00 makes the condition False, so the assert stops the script with its message.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check every price against `p > 0`.

explain.text: £0.00 is not above zero, so `all(...)` is False. The assert raises `AssertionError` with the text after the comma, and `loaded` never prints. Catching the zero here stops a division by zero later.

items.question: Select all that apply: which does pytest collect and run?

options.why: You applied the file rule to a function. Function names must start with `test`.
`check_` is not `test`. pytest never calls it.

feedback.correct: Every name that starts with `test` runs, even `testing_helper`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. pytest calls every function whose name starts with the letters `test`.

byKey.helper: `testing_helper` starts with the letters `test`, so pytest calls it as a test. Name helpers so they do not.

explain.text: pytest matches the start of the name, letter by letter. `testing_helper` begins with `test`, so it runs as a test whether you meant it or not. `signal_test` and `check_short_signal` never run.

items.prose: A bug makes `daily_returns` read the prices in reverse order.
items.question: Which assert catches the bug?

options.why: Your prices read the same backwards. Reversing them changes nothing, so the bug passes.
A flat path reads the same both ways. Every return is 0.0 in either order.
Reversing keeps the count. Both orders give two returns.

feedback.correct: Reversed, a steady rise turns into falls.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For each assert, reverse its prices and see whether the answer changes.

explain.text: Reversed, £121.00, £110.00, £100.00 gives two falls of about 9.09%, so the assert fails. The other inputs read the same both ways, or the check ignores order. A good test input breaks the symmetry the bug relies on.

items.prose: A test for `max_drawdown`, the largest fall from a peak as a fraction of it.
items.question: Put the lines in arrange, act, assert order.

feedback.correct: Prices, one call, then the check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each line needs what the line above it made.

explain.text: Arrange the prices, act by calling `max_drawdown` once, assert against the hand answer. From the £125.00 peak to £100.00 is 25 / 125 = 0.2.

options.text: The code: the fall from £120.00 to £90.00 is 0.25
The test: the path ends above £90.00, so there is no drawdown
options.why: A drawdown is the worst fall on the way, even if the price recovers later. £120.00 to £90.00 is a fall of 0.25.

options.text: Neither: it is a floating-point slip
options.why: 0.0 against 0.25 is far too big for a slip.
A crash ends in an error other than `AssertionError`. Here the code returned 0.0.

feedback.correct: £30.00 down from a £120.00 peak is 0.25. The code missed it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the drawdown yourself, then compare it with each side.

explain.text: The peak is £120.00 and the low after it is £90.00: 30 / 120 = 0.25. The code returned 0.0, so the code is wrong. Perhaps it only looks for peaks after the first price.

```text
    def test_bad_file():
>       r = daily_returns([100.00, 0.00, 105.00])

returns.py:3: in daily_returns
    return [(b - a) / a for a, b in zip(prices, prices[1:])]
E   ZeroDivisionError: float division by zero
```
items.question: What does this report tell you?

options.text: The code crashed on the £0.00 price, an edge case it does not handle

options.why: A wrong number ends in `AssertionError` with both values. Here no value came back at all.
A typo gives a `NameError` in the test file. This error comes from inside `returns.py`.

options.text: Nothing: the test has no assert, so it is not a real failure
options.why: Any error fails a test. The crash inside `daily_returns` is what failed it.

feedback.correct: The crash is inside `daily_returns`, on the zero price.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read where the error was raised and what kind it is.

explain.text: The report walks from the test into `returns.py`, line 3, where `105.00 / 0.00` raised. So the code itself fails on a zero price. Deciding what it should do instead, such as raising a clear `ValueError`, is the next design choice.

items.prose: A test checks a portfolio worth £1,000,000.00. A pricing bug that is £1.00 out must fail, but a rounding slip far below a penny must pass.
items.question: Which assert does that?

options.why: The default gap is relative: a millionth of £1,000,000.00 is £1.00, so the bug passes.
`rel=0.005` is half a percent of the value: £5,000.00. The bug passes easily.
Exact equality fails on the rounding slip too.

feedback.correct: A fixed gap of half a penny, whatever the size of the book.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out the gap each assert allows on £1,000,000.00.

explain.text: Given only `abs=0.005`, approx drops its relative gap and allows exactly half a penny either side. So the £1.00 bug fails and the slip passes. pytest prints the rule it used: `1000000.0 ± 0.005`.

items.prose: `total_return(prices)` gives the return from the first price to the last. On paper two 10% rises make 21%. In floats `121.00 / 100.00 - 1` is `0.20999999999999996`. The starter's first lines stand in for pytest.
items.question: Write `test_two_rises` so it passes on correct versions and fails on broken ones.

tests.setup: total_return = lambda prices: sum((b - a) / a for a, b in zip(prices, prices[1:]))

widget.how: Check runs your test against two correct versions, where it must pass, and against four broken versions, where it must fail.

feedback.correct: Your test passes both correct versions and fails every bug.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read which version your test let through or rejected.

byKey.test-1: Your test fails on the right code. `0.20999999999999996` is not `0.21` under `==`: use `pytest.approx(0.21)`.
byKey.test-3: The version that adds the daily returns got through. It gives 0.2, not 0.21: keep the default tolerance.
byKey.error: Your code stopped before the tests could run. Read the error under the editor.

explain.text:
£121.00 / £100.00 − 1 = 0.21 on paper, and approx accepts the float slip. Adding the two daily returns gives 0.2, which misses compounding, and approx still rejects it.

```python
def test_two_rises():
    assert total_return([100.00, 110.00, 121.00]) == pytest.approx(0.21)
```
